content: Bronchitis refers to the inflammation of the bronchi, which are the medium and large-sized airways in the respiratory system. There are two primary forms of bronchitis: acute bronchitis and chronic bronchitis. Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting condition typically caused by viral or bacterial infections. In contrast, chronic bronchitis is a distinct medical condition that falls under the umbrella of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Chronic bronchitis is clinically defined as a productive cough that persists for at least three months in two consecutive years. The inflammatory response in bronchitis involves the bronchial epithelium reacting to infections or irritants, which leads to thickening of the mucosal lining in the bronchi and trachea. In chronic bronchitis, key pathological features include hyperplasia (increased number) and hypertrophy (enlargement) of goblet cells in the airway. This results in excessive mucus production, which contributes to airway obstruction. Microscopically, the airway walls show infiltration by inflammatory cells, particularly neutrophils. Over time, this inflammation leads to scarring and remodeling of the airway walls, causing them to thicken and narrow, especially in the smaller airways. As the disease progresses, metaplasia (abnormal transformation of cells) and fibrosis (formation of scar tissue) occur in the lower airways, further limiting airflow. Acute bronchitis is more commonly observed in young children and older adults, with an overall incidence of approximately 5% in the United States. It does not show a preference for any specific race or gender. However, chronic bronchitis is more prevalent among older adults and is more commonly seen in Caucasian individuals compared to other racial groups, though it affects males and females equally. Several factors influence the risk of developing acute bronchitis, including age, seasonal variations, and immunization status. The most significant risk factor for chronic bronchitis is cigarette smoking. Acute bronchitis is characterized by a lower respiratory tract infection that typically presents with a cough lasting up to three weeks. It is generally self-limiting and resolves without significant complications. On the other hand, chronic bronchitis is a progressive condition that worsens over time and can ultimately lead to death. The rate of disease progression varies among individuals and is influenced by the degree of airflow obstruction. Early recognition of the condition and smoking cessation are critical for improving outcomes. Bronchitis is classified into two main categories based on the duration and chronicity of symptoms: 1.
